name: Fatima
short_meaning: One who abstains, one who weans
primary_meaning: Fatima (Arabic فَاطِمَة, Fāṭimah) is an Arabic female name whose literal meaning is “one who separates” or “one who abstains”, from the root F-Ṭ-M, “to wean, to separate”. It is borne most famously by Fatimah bint Muhammad, the daughter of the Prophet.
literal_meaning: One who separates / abstains; one who weans (active participle of faṭama)
meaning_explanation: Fāṭimah is a feminine active participle of the Arabic root F-Ṭ-M (ف ط م), “to separate, to cut one thing from another” — the ordinary word for weaning a child. Islamic tradition reads the name of the Prophet's daughter as “one kept separate from evil” or “from Hell”, an interpretation drawn from narrations rather than from the dictionary sense.

etymology.morphology: Feminine active participle (fāʿila pattern) of faṭama, “to wean, to separate”.
etymology.explanation: Derived from F-Ṭ-M, meaning “to separate, to cut something from another”.

origin.explanation: Arabic, used throughout the Muslim world. Spoken Levantine and Egyptian Arabic and Turkish shorten it to Fatma; Persian has Fatemeh, Tajik Fotima, Azerbaijani Fatimə and South India Fathima.

religion.association: Islamic — name of the Prophet's daughter
religion.explanation: Fatimah bint Muhammad was the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, wife of Ali ibn Abi Talib and mother of Hasan and Husayn. She is honoured by all Muslims and is especially central in Shia devotion; she is known by titles such as al-Zahra (“the radiant”) and al-Batul.

naming_context.context: One of the most common female names in the Muslim world, often paired with her titles — Fatima Zahra, Fatima Batool.
naming_context.interpretation: Parents choose it to honour the Prophet's daughter.
naming_context.important_distinction: The reading “separated from Hell” comes from traditions about why she was given the name; the literal dictionary sense is “one who weans/separates”.

cultural.meaning: Her titles have become names in their own right — Zahra (“luminous, radiant”) and Batul (“ascetic”).
cultural.impact: The Portuguese town of Fátima — and through it the Catholic shrine of Our Lady of Fátima — is named after a Moorish princess called Fatima.

items: Borne by several relatives of the Prophet Muhammad, most famously his daughter Fatimah.
The Fatimid Caliphate (909–1171) took its name from her, claiming descent through her.
history.person: Fatimah bint Muhammad, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad.

modern_usage: Used across the whole Muslim world in many local spellings; Fatma is the usual Turkish form.

english.name: Fatima
english.meaning: One who abstains; one who weans

urdu.name: فاطمہ
urdu.meaning: دودھ چھڑانے والی، الگ رہنے والی

pronunciation.note: The ṭ is an emphatic Arabic t; colloquial Arabic and Turkish drop the middle vowel (Fatma).

variant_notes: Fatma (Turkish/colloquial Arabic), Fatemeh (Persian), Fathima (South India), Fotima (Tajik).

faq.a: Literally “one who separates” or “one who abstains”, from the Arabic root F-Ṭ-M, “to wean, to separate”.
Fatimah bint Muhammad, the Prophet's daughter, wife of Ali ibn Abi Talib and mother of Hasan and Husayn.

faq.q: Why is Fatima linked with being “kept from Hell”?
faq.a: Traditions narrate that she was named Fatimah because God separated her and her followers from the Fire; this is a religious interpretation of the name, beyond its dictionary sense.

faq.q: What is the Turkish form of Fatima?
faq.a: Fatma, which also reflects the colloquial Arabic pronunciation. Fadime is a less common variant.

faq.q: What titles of Fatima are used as names?
faq.a: Zahra (“luminous, radiant”) and Batul (“ascetic”), often combined as Fatima Zahra.

faq.q: Why is there a town called Fátima in Portugal?
faq.a: The Portuguese town is named after a Moorish princess called Fatima; the Catholic shrine of Our Lady of Fátima takes its name from the town.

Fatma is the colloquial and Turkish form; Fatemeh Persian, Fathima South Asian, Fotima Tajik.
Her titles include Zahra (luminous; radiant) and Batul.
Fatimah was the daughter of Muhammad, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.
The Fatimid Caliphate claimed descent from her.
